## The question, and what an answer looks like {.unnumbered}

Rotor-speed regressors trained on the stochastic synthetic family alone score
8.1 rev/s MAE on the real panel; the same architectures trained with real
audio in the mix score 2.7. Every attempt to close that gap so far has moved
one range of the sampler at a time (floor level, comb length, band edge,
flicker) and measured whether transfer improved. None did. That leaves two
hypotheses standing, and they call for opposite fixes:

* **H1 — wrong ranges.** The family *contains* good models of real rotor
  noise, but the sampler rarely draws them. Fix: retune the sampler.
* **H2 — wrong family.** No member of the family looks like real rotor noise:
  some structural assumption (line shape, width law, common floor, Gaussian
  statistics, independent-per-microphone realizations, …) is false. Fix:
  change the model.

The only way to separate them is to find the *best* member of the family for
a given real recording and measure how far it still is from the recording.
That is a **fit**. This document defines exactly what will be fitted, what
quantity will be minimized, how the minimized number will be turned into an
answer to H1-vs-H2, and why each engineering step of the procedure is there.

Reading guide: §@sec-prereq is the textbook part (spectra, Gaussian processes,
likelihoods, MAP). §@sec-model writes the generative model down completely.
§@sec-objective states the objective. §@sec-scale explains how one likelihood
number becomes "how much is explained". §@sec-procedure is the procedure and
its engineering. §@sec-reading is what each possible outcome would mean.

## Prerequisites {#sec-prereq}

### Spectrogram cells as random variables {#sec-periodogram}

Take one microphone's audio $x[n]$ at 16 kHz, a Hann window $w$ of 2048
samples (128 ms) and a hop of 512. The short-time Fourier transform is

$$
X(t, f) = \sum_{n} w[n]\, x[n + 512\,t]\, e^{-2\pi i f n / 2048},
\qquad f = 0, 1, \dots, 1024 \text{ (bins of 7.8125 Hz)} .
$$

The **periodogram** is its power, normalized so that white noise of variance
$\sigma^2$ gives cells of mean $\sigma^2$:

$$
I(t, f) = \frac{|X(t,f)|^2}{\sum_n w[n]^2} .
$$

This is exactly the front end every RPS model in the project sees, so a
mismatch measured on this grid is the mismatch the models experience.

The key fact for everything that follows: **if $x$ is a Gaussian process**
(any signal that is a linear filtering of white Gaussian noise — which is
precisely what the renderer produces), then each $X(t,f)$ is a complex
Gaussian variable with mean zero and some variance $M(t,f)$, and therefore

$$
I(t,f) \sim \operatorname{Exponential}\big(\text{mean } M(t,f)\big),
\qquad p(I \mid M) = \frac{1}{M} e^{-I/M} .
$$ {#eq-exp}

$M(t,f)$ is the **expected periodogram**: the signal's power spectral density
at $(t, f)$, smeared by the window. For a stationary spectrum $S(f)$ on the
bin grid, a periodic Hann window mixes each bin with its neighbours through
its own power response,

$$
M(f) = \tfrac16 S(f{-}1) + \tfrac23 S(f) + \tfrac16 S(f{+}1),
$$ {#eq-kernel}

because the Hann window's DFT has exactly three non-zero coefficients
$(-\tfrac14, \tfrac12, -\tfrac14)$ and power adds their squares. A model of
the *spectrum* must therefore be pushed through @eq-kernel before it is
compared to the periodogram; otherwise a line narrower than a bin is
predicted 33 % too tall at its peak and absent in its neighbours.

Two approximations are being made and should be named. Adjacent frames
overlap by 75 %, so cells one hop apart are not independent — for a Hann
window the correlation of their *powers* is about 0.03, small enough to
ignore. Adjacent bins are correlated more strongly (about 0.44), which does
not bias anything below but means the effective number of independent cells
is roughly two thirds of the count; every score is reported per cell, so this
only affects how one would put error bars on it.

### The Whittle likelihood {#sec-whittle}

Given a model spectrum $M$ with parameters $\theta$, the log-likelihood of one
cell under @eq-exp is $-\log M - I/M$. Summing over cells and flipping the
sign gives the **Whittle negative log-likelihood**:

$$
\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \sum_{m,t,f} \left[ \frac{I_m(t,f)}{M_m(t,f;\theta)} + \log M_m(t,f;\theta) \right] .
$$ {#eq-whittle}

Read the two terms as forces on $M$: the ratio $I/M$ pushes $M$ *up* wherever
the model predicts less power than observed (a line the model does not have
costs $I/M \gg 1$); the logarithm pushes $M$ *down* everywhere, so the model
cannot buy its way out by predicting huge power. The per-cell minimum is at
$M = I$, where the cost is $1 + \log I$; a model that is *correct*, i.e. has
$M$ equal to the true expectation, does not reach that minimum on any single
cell (the cell is random), but reaches the smallest *expected* cost,
$1 + \log M_{\text{true}}$. The difference between a model's expected cost and
that floor is the Kullback–Leibler divergence between the two exponential
laws:

$$
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\tfrac{I}{M} + \log M\right] - \big(1 + \log M_{\text{true}}\big)
= \frac{M_{\text{true}}}{M} - 1 - \log\frac{M_{\text{true}}}{M} \;\ge\; 0 ,
$$ {#eq-kl}

zero only when $M = M_{\text{true}}$. Every excess-over-truth number in this
document is this quantity averaged over cells: **nats per cell**, a
unit-free measure of how wrong the model's predicted power is, on average.

```{ojs}
//| label: fig-whittle
//| fig-cap: "The per-cell excess cost of predicting M when the truth is M_true, as a function of the ratio. Predicting half the true power costs 0.31 nats; predicting double costs 0.19; both directions are penalized, under-prediction harder."
viewof ratioPick = Inputs.range([0.1, 5], {value: 2, step: 0.05, label: "M / M_true"})
```

```{ojs}
{
  const kl = r => 1/r - 1 + Math.log(r);
  const pts = d3.range(0.1, 5.001, 0.02).map(r => ({r, kl: kl(r)}));
  return Plot.plot({
    width: 640, height: 300, x: {label: "M / M_true", type: "log"}, y: {label: "excess cost, nats/cell"},
    marks: [Plot.line(pts, {x: "r", y: "kl"}), Plot.dot([{r: ratioPick, kl: kl(ratioPick)}], {x: "r", y: "kl", r: 5, fill: "crimson"}),
            Plot.text([{r: ratioPick, kl: kl(ratioPick)}], {x: "r", y: "kl", text: d => d.kl.toFixed(3) + " nats", dy: -12})]
  });
}
```

Why not least squares on the spectrogram in dB? Because @eq-exp is not
symmetric in dB: the periodogram of a *correct* model scatters by $-\ln 2 =
-1.6$ dB at the median and has a long upper tail, so an L1/L2 fit in dB
converges to the wrong level (the project already paid for this lesson in the
wind-channel work). The Whittle cost is the likelihood the data actually
follow.

### Gaussian processes as priors on slow curves {#sec-gp}

The renderer makes every line's log-power drift in time as a **Gaussian
process** (GP): a random function $h(t)$ whose values at any set of times are
jointly Gaussian with covariance

$$
\operatorname{Cov}\big(h(t), h(t')\big) = \sigma^2 \exp\!\left(-\frac{(t-t')^2}{2\tau^2}\right) ,
$$

the squared-exponential kernel: $\sigma$ is how far the curve wanders (dB),
$\tau$ how slowly (s). On a grid of knot times $t_1 \dots t_J$ this is a
$J \times J$ covariance matrix $K$, and a draw is $h = L z$ with $L L^\top = K$
(the Cholesky factor) and $z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$. Two consequences:

* **Prior as penalty.** $-\log p(h) = \tfrac12 h^\top K^{-1} h + \text{const}
  = \tfrac12 \|z\|^2$. Parametrizing the curve by its *whitened* coordinates
  $z$ turns the GP prior into a plain ridge penalty, and the optimizer sees a
  well-conditioned problem.
* **Fixed hyperparameters.** With $\sigma, \tau$ fixed, the constant above
  really is constant. If they were fitted jointly with $z$, the term
  $\tfrac12 \log\det K$ would have to be included, and joint optimization of
  latents and their own prior scale is degenerate (it drives $\sigma \to 0$).
  So the fit holds $\sigma, \tau$ at the family's midpoints (3 dB, 1.5 s) and
  afterwards *measures* the standard deviation and correlation time of the
  fitted curves; those measured values are what is compared to the sampler's
  ranges.

### MAP estimation {#sec-map}

The unknowns split into **parameters** $\theta$ (levels, widths, floor shape,
gains — a few hundred numbers that the sampler draws once per clip) and
**latent curves** $z$ (the drifts — thousands of numbers that the renderer
draws from the GPs). Bayes:

$$
p(\theta, z \mid I) \propto p(I \mid \theta, z)\; p(z)\; p(\theta) .
$$

The **maximum a posteriori** (MAP) estimate is the $(\theta, z)$ minimizing
$-\log p(I \mid \theta, z) - \log p(z) - \log p(\theta)$. No prior is placed on
$\theta$ (flat), so the parameters are maximum-likelihood; the latents carry
the GP prior. This is a *joint* MAP: it picks one drift curve per line
instead of averaging over all curves compatible with the data (the marginal
likelihood). The joint estimate is the appropriate one here because the
fitted curves themselves are an output — their statistics are what gets
compared to the sampler — and because the marginal would require integrating
a log-power GP through an exponential likelihood, which has no closed form.

One consequence to keep in mind when reading fitted curves: MAP curves are
*smoother than truth*. Where the data barely constrain a line (a faint
harmonic), the prior wins and the curve sits near zero; the fitted standard
deviation of a faint line's drift underestimates the real drift.

## The generative model, completely {#sec-model}

This is `data_processing.stochastic_rotor_noise` written as equations, with
the renderer's names. Rotor speeds $r_\rho(t)$, $\rho = 1..R$ (rev/s), are
*given* — from telemetry refined against the audio's low harmonics — and are
held fixed throughout the fit. $k$ indexes harmonic order, $m$ microphones.

**Lines.** Harmonic $k$ of rotor $\rho$ is a Lorentzian line centred at
$k\,r_\rho(t)$ with half-width at half-maximum $\gamma_{\rho k}$ and power
$P_{\rho k}(t)$ (unit-area density times power):

$$
\ell_{\rho k}(f, t) = P_{\rho k}(t)\, \frac{1}{\pi}\frac{\gamma_{\rho k}}{(f - k r_\rho(t))^2 + \gamma_{\rho k}^2} .
$$ {#eq-line}

A Lorentzian is what a tone with a random-walk phase produces; its width is a
*frequency* jitter, hence the linear width law
$\gamma_{\rho k} = \gamma_{0\rho} + s_\rho\, k$ (a shaft wandering by 0.6
rev/s widens harmonic $k$ by about $0.6k$ Hz).

**Line power.** In decibels, everything is additive:

$$
10\log_{10} P_{\rho k}(t) = \underbrace{\pi_{\rho k}}_{\text{static profile}}
+ \underbrace{h_{\rho k}(t)}_{\text{GP drift}}
+ \underbrace{10\,\alpha \log_{10}\!\frac{r_\rho(t)}{80}}_{\text{speed law, } \alpha = 2.5} .
$$ {#eq-power}

The renderer builds the profile $\pi$ from a roll-off $-10 p \log_{10} k$,
a blade-passing emphasis on every $b$-th order, per-order jitter, and a
clip-wide mean; the fit does not need that decomposition — it estimates
$\pi_{\rho k}$ freely, one number per line, and the roll-off / jitter are
*read off* the fitted profile afterwards. The drift is
$h_{\rho k} = \sqrt{\varrho}\, c_\rho + \sqrt{1-\varrho}\, e_{\rho k}$, a
per-rotor common GP mixed with a private one; either way $h_{\rho k}$ is a GP
with the same $\sigma, \tau$, which is how the fit treats it (the common /
private split is again measured on the fitted curves).

**Floor.** The broadband part, in dB:

$$
\begin{aligned}
10\log_{10} B_0(f,t) &= \beta_0 + \beta(f) + b(t) + \big(\theta_0 + \theta(t)\big)\log_2\!\frac{f}{500\,\text{Hz}} , \\
B(f,t) &= B_0(f,t) \cdot \Big[\tfrac1R \textstyle\sum_\rho \big(\tfrac{r_\rho(t)}{80}\big)^{\alpha_B} + s_0\Big] ,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-floor}

with $\beta(f)$ a smooth random curve through 14 control points spaced in
log-frequency, $b(t)$ and $\theta(t)$ slow GPs (level and tilt drift), and a
speed factor: the rotors' share of the floor scales like the lines, plus a
static share $s_0$ (the recording chain's own floor, what remains when the
rotors stop).

**Microphones.** Each microphone $m$ hears the same floor and the lines of
rotor $\rho$ through a gain $g_{m\rho}$ (drawn uniformly in $[-12, 0]$ dB):

$$
S_m(f, t) = B(f,t) + \sum_\rho g_{m\rho} \sum_k \ell_{\rho k}(f,t) .
$$ {#eq-spectrum}

**Realization.** For each microphone independently, white Gaussian noise is
filtered in the STFT domain with gain $\sqrt{S_m}$ and overlap-added; the
clip is then scaled to a fixed RMS. Two things follow. First, the output is
(before the RMS scaling) a Gaussian process with spectrum $S_m$, so
§@sec-periodogram applies and its periodogram cells are exponential with mean
$S_m$ smeared by @eq-kernel. Second, the microphones are *independent
realizations* — there is no cross-microphone phase relation — and the fit,
which uses one likelihood per microphone, is blind to that assumption by
construction. Cross-microphone structure is not part of this question.

**What the fit therefore estimates**, given $r_\rho(t)$:

| symbol | meaning | count (4 rotors, $K$ orders, 8 mics, $J$ knots) |
|---|---|---|
| $\pi_{\rho k}$ | static line levels (dB) | $4K$ |
| $z_{\rho k}$ | whitened drift knots, $h = \sigma L z$ | $4KJ$ |
| $\gamma_{0\rho}, s_\rho$ | width law (Hz, Hz/order) | 8 |
| $\beta_0, \beta_{1..14}, \theta_0$ | floor level, shape, tilt | 16 |
| $z^b, z^\theta$ | floor level / tilt drift knots | $2J$ |
| $g_{m\rho}$ | microphone line gains (dB), mean over $m$ pinned to 0 | 32 |
| $\alpha, \alpha_B, s_0$ | speed law (fixed at 2.5, 2.5, 0 unless a clip has speed variation) | 3 |

For a 4 s crop at 30 rev/s, $K = 266$ orders reach the 8 kHz band edge and
$J = 41$ knots (0.1 s spacing): about 45 000 numbers, 96 % of them drift
knots, fitted to $8 \times 122 \times 1021 \approx 10^6$ periodogram cells.

## The objective {#sec-objective}

Put @eq-line–@eq-spectrum on the bin grid. Two details make the model
predict the periodogram rather than the density: each line's density is
*integrated across its bin* (the Lorentzian's antiderivative is an arctangent,
so this is exact and cheap), which keeps a sub-bin-wide line's power right
whatever its sub-bin position; and the whole spectrum is convolved with the
Hann kernel @eq-kernel. Call the result $M_m(t,f;\theta,z)$. The fit
minimizes

$$
\begin{aligned}
J(\theta, z) \;=\;& \sum_{m}\sum_{t}\sum_{f \in \text{band}}
\left[ \frac{I_m(t,f)}{M_m(t,f;\theta,z)} + \log M_m(t,f;\theta,z) \right] \\
&+\; \tfrac12 \|z\|^2 \;+\; \tfrac12 \|z^b\|^2 + \tfrac12 \|z^\theta\|^2 + \tfrac12\|z^\beta\|^2
\;+\; \tfrac{1}{2\sigma_r^2}\|\delta\|^2 ,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-objective}

term by term:

* the Whittle sum @eq-whittle over the fit band (30 Hz to Nyquist; below
  30 Hz a 16 kHz recording carries nothing and the renderer holds its floor
  flat), all microphones, all frames of the clip;
* the GP priors of the line drifts, the floor's level and tilt drifts, and
  the floor's 14-point shape (a GP in log-frequency, as in the sampler);
* optionally (variant `family_rps`) a smooth per-rotor **carrier correction**
  $\delta_\rho(t)$ added to the given speeds, on a 0.5 s knot grid with a
  0.3 rev/s prior. Its purpose is defensive: the references are acoustic
  refinements, not tachometers, and an error of 0.3 rev/s misplaces
  harmonic 100 by 30 Hz, four bins, which a fit with the correct widths would
  otherwise have to explain by *widening* the lines. The prior keeps it a
  correction, not a search.

Nothing else is regularized. The periodogram is scaled to unit mean before
the fit, which shifts every score of a clip by the same constant and keeps
the arithmetic in float32 range.

Reported score: the Whittle sum divided by the number of band cells,
**nats per cell**, for the fitted model. On its own that number is
meaningless — it depends on the clip's spectrum through $\log M$. It becomes
meaningful against two references.

## From a likelihood to "how much is explained" {#sec-scale}

Two reference scores bracket every fit on the same cells:

**Bottom of the scale — floor only.** The same model with all lines switched
off, fitted to the same clip: level, shape, tilt and drifts of the floor
alone. Its score $\mathcal{L}_\text{floor}$ is what "no comb at all"
achieves. Anything a comb model gains is measured from here.

**Top of the scale — leave-one-out smoother.** For each cell, predict its
expectation by the mean of its four time-neighbours (same bin, same
microphone, frames $t\pm1, t\pm2$):

$$
\hat M(t,f) = \tfrac14\big[I(t{-}2,f) + I(t{-}1,f) + I(t{+}1,f) + I(t{+}2,f)\big] .
$$

For a locally stationary process these are four replicates of the cell, so
$\hat M$ is an unbiased estimate of $M_\text{true}$ that uses **no model at
all**. Scoring the cell against $\hat M$ costs a little more than scoring it
against the true $M$ because $\hat M$ is itself noisy; for exponential cells
that bias is analytic — $\mathbb{E}[I/\hat M] = n/(n-1)$ and
$\mathbb{E}[\log \hat M] = \log M + \psi(n) - \log n$ — and is subtracted,
giving $\mathcal{L}_\text{LOO}$, an estimate of $1 + \log M_\text{true}$
averaged over cells: **the score a correct model would reach**. The
approximation is stationarity over $\pm 2$ hops (64 ms); on a ramp whose
lines move by more than a bin over that span the smoother is optimistic,
which is why each fit records how far its fastest in-band line moves over
the neighbourhood and why the near-steady crops carry the headline numbers.

With both, a fit with score $\mathcal{L}_\text{fit}$ yields

$$
\text{explained} = \frac{\mathcal{L}_\text{floor} - \mathcal{L}_\text{fit}}{\mathcal{L}_\text{floor} - \mathcal{L}_\text{LOO}} ,
\qquad
\text{excess} = \mathcal{L}_\text{fit} - \mathcal{L}_\text{LOO} \;\approx\; \overline{\mathrm{KL}}\big(\text{truth}\,\|\,\text{fit}\big) \text{ nats/cell.}
$$

*Explained* is a fraction of the way from "no comb" to "correct"; *excess* is
the absolute residual misfit in the units of @eq-kl, which can be localized
to cells (§@sec-diagnostics). Both are computed for every variant of the
model on every clip, and on renderer-generated control clips where the
answer is known (explained ≈ 1, excess ≈ 0 up to the LOO's own noise).

## The procedure and its engineering {#sec-procedure}

### Data {#sec-data}

* **Real, near-steady:** the 27 four-second training crops of the linewidth
  audit (17 DREGON room2, 10 Michael's FLY125), eight channels, telemetry
  refined against the low harmonics. These carry the headline numbers.
* **Real, full regime:** the `nosource` clips of the frozen validation split
  (DREGON room1 with *measured* shaft rate, Michael's FLY124), eight seconds
  each, including stopped rotors, spin-ups and ramps — the frames where
  synthetic-only models fail worst. Refined the same way where the rotors
  turn; telemetry otherwise.
* **Synthetic controls:** renderer draws on the real trajectories, with the
  planted parameters kept. A fit that cannot recover planted widths and
  profiles on these says nothing about real audio.

### Initialization {#sec-init}

@eq-objective is not convex: a line placed on the wrong neighbour, a width
twice too large, a floor that has swallowed the comb are all local minima.
The starting point is therefore chosen from the data, crudely but safely:

* floor level from the 20th percentile of the periodogram over time in each
  bin (+6.5 dB, the exponential law's correction for a 20th percentile:
  between lines the floor dominates and lines move, so the percentile sees
  the floor);
* each line's level from the median periodogram at its centre bin minus the
  floor, divided by the peak density a line of the starting width has;
* widths at the family's midpoint ($\gamma_0 = 2$ Hz, $s = 0.3$ Hz/order),
  gains 0 dB, all drifts zero.

### Stages {#sec-stages}

1. **Floor only** (lines off) — Adam then L-BFGS. Its optimum *is* the
   floor-only reference of §@sec-scale; nothing is fitted twice.
2. **Harmonic ladder** — lines on up to order 16, then 48, then all, 150
   Adam steps per rung. Low orders are well resolved (a 0.3 rev/s carrier
   error is 5 Hz at $k=16$, under a bin) and anchor the width law and any
   carrier correction before the crowded high orders — where neighbouring
   rotors' lines overlap and a wrong carrier can be traded for a wider line —
   are allowed to pull.
3. **Polish** — all parameters, 300 Adam steps, then 60 L-BFGS iterations
   with a strong-Wolfe line search for the last digits.

Adam is used first because the parameters live on very different scales
(decibels, hertz, whitened knots) and its per-coordinate step handles that
without hand-tuned preconditioning; L-BFGS finishes because near the optimum
its curvature model converges far faster than a first-order method.

### Cost and where it runs {#sec-compute}

The expensive tensor is the line spectrum before summing over orders:
rotors × orders × frames × bins = $4 \times 266 \times 122 \times 1025
\approx 1.3\times10^8$ values per evaluation, with gradients. It is
evaluated in chunks of 32 orders on a GPU; one iteration takes well under a
second on a P100/T4, so one variant of one clip takes a few minutes. The fits
run as omnirun jobs on Kaggle/Colab from a slim source snapshot (the job
imports only this package; the renderer and the tracker run once, on a CPU
job, to build the clip bundle on R2). The laptop is not used for the
optimization.

### Variants: one structural change at a time {#sec-variants}

Every variant is the family plus exactly one relaxation, so its gain over
`family_rps` is the price of that one assumption:

| variant | what changes | which assumption it tests |
|---|---|---|
| `family` | nothing | the family as the sampler draws it |
| `family_rps` | + carrier correction $\delta_\rho(t)$ | reference accuracy (a nuisance, removed before reading the rest) |
| `free_gamma` | $\gamma_{\rho k}$ free per line (smooth in $k$) | the linear width law $\gamma_0 + s k$ |
| `gauss` | Gaussian line of the same HWHM | the Lorentzian shape (a Gaussian is what *speed* jitter within a frame produces; a Lorentzian is phase jitter) |
| `mic_floor` | + per-microphone floor offset | the common floor |
| `speed_law` | $\alpha, \alpha_B, s_0$ fitted | the $r^{2.5}$ law and the static floor share (only identifiable on ramps) |
| `extended` | all of the above | the most the family's *shape* can be stretched — the ceiling of H1-style fixes |

### Diagnostics: where the excess lives {#sec-diagnostics}

The fitted spectrum gives a residual field $\;R_m(t,f) = I_m(t,f) / M_m(t,f)$,
which under a correct model is exponential with mean 1 everywhere and no
structure. Its structure, read along the fitted lines, localizes the misfit:

* **Line profile.** $R$ sampled at offsets $d$ from each line centre, in
  units of that line's fitted $\gamma$, averaged over time, microphones and
  the lines of an order band (1–8, 9–24, 25–64, 65+). A peak at $d = 0$ with
  troughs at the shoulders means the true line is *narrower* or *sharper*
  than the Lorentzian fitted to it (a coherent core); the opposite, wider.
  This is the direct test of the linewidth question the 2026-09-06 audits
  could not settle.
* **Temporal structure.** Autocorrelation of $\log R$ at line centres over
  frames. A correct drift model leaves white residuals; slow structure means
  the GP's $\tau$ or $\sigma$ are wrong, or the drift is not Gaussian.
* **Coherence.** The normalized variance of $R$ at line centres,
  $\operatorname{Var}(R)/\mathbb{E}[R]^2$, is 1 for exponential cells and
  drops toward 0 for a steady tone in noise (Rician). Per order band, this
  measures how much of each harmonic is a *tone* rather than narrowband
  noise — the `stochastic` vs `coherent` line-mode question, as a number per
  order, calibrated on the synthetic controls.
* **Between the lines.** Mean $R$ at the midpoints between adjacent orders,
  against frequency: floor shape errors. And at half-integer orders: lines
  the family does not have.
* **Per microphone.** Mean $R$ per microphone on line cells versus floor
  cells: whether an 8-channel real recording has a common floor.
* **Fitted parameters against the sampler.** Roll-off $p$ and jitter from a
  regression of $\pi_{\rho k}$ on $\log_{10} k$; $\gamma_0, s$; floor level
  under the median line peak; the standard deviation and correlation time of
  the fitted $h_{\rho k}(t)$; the common/private variance split; microphone
  gain spread; tilt — each placed against the range the sampler draws it
  from.

### Controls that must pass first {#sec-controls}

On the synthetic clips: planted $\gamma_0, s$, profile roll-off and microphone
gains recovered within their identifiable precision; explained fraction at
1 within the LOO's noise; residual profile flat. If these fail, the procedure
— not the family — is wrong, and nothing from real clips is read.

## Reading the outcome {#sec-reading}

| observation on real clips | reading | consequence |
|---|---|---|
| `family` explains ≳ 0.9 with a flat residual profile, and the fitted parameters fall *outside* the sampler's ranges | H1: right family, wrong ranges | retune the ranges from the fitted distributions; posterior-predictive check; retrain S2 |
| `family` explains ≳ 0.9 and the fitted parameters fall *inside* the ranges | the spectrum is not where the transfer gap is | the gap is in what the Whittle fit is blind to: cross-microphone structure, non-Gaussian statistics (coherence), or the trajectory distribution — the coherence diagnostic and the array are next |
| `family` leaves a large excess but one variant (`free_gamma`, `gauss`, `mic_floor`) removes most of it | H2, localized | that structural change goes into the renderer; the fitted parameters then say the ranges |
| even `extended` leaves a large, structured excess | H2, unlocalized within this family | the residual profile / half-order / coherence diagnostics say what kind of component is missing; the family is not the model of real rotor noise |

"Large" is calibrated by the synthetic controls' own excess and by the KL
scale of @eq-kl: 0.1 nats/cell is a 60 % power error on every cell, or a
factor of 10 on one cell in fifteen.
